title: Federal ACT Labor MP sounds alarm over potential $1b funding black hole
excerpt: David Smith says self-government funding deals have not kept up.
content:
The ACT might be missing out on as much as $1.8 billion a year from the federal government because funding promises made when the territory was forced to govern itself have not maintained their value, a federal Labor MP says.

Federal Labor MP David Smith, who argues the ACT is missing out on funding from the federal government promised at self government. Picture by Keegan Carroll

David Smith said funding arrangements for the capital needed reviewing and key assumptions made in 1988 as the territory's system of government were devised by federal parliamentarians had worn thin.

"The Commonwealth funds about 44 per cent of the territory's state-type services. It funds 60 per cent of Tasmania's," Mr Smith's submission to an ACT parliamentary inquiry examining electoral representation said.

"In 1988 the Commonwealth's own Grants Commission assessed that funding the ACT as it funded the states would mean the Commonwealth meeting about two-thirds of the cost of those services, and 65 per cent was the benchmark the responsible minister put to Canberrans.

"On an indicative comparison using the method described in this submission, the difference may be in order of $1.3 billion to $1.8 billion a year, comparable to the territory's $1.4 billion operating deficit in 2024-25 and several times its $323 million headline deficit."

The figures were an approximation and a review would be more accurate but the gap measured in billions could not be closed by refinement alone, he said.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr told the inquiry the government believed the size of the Assembly should be reviewed when the ACT population approaches 600,000 residents and "parliamentary productivity, capability and scrutiny reforms should be prioritised before consideration is given to increasing the size of the Legislative Assembly".

The ACT Greens said the Assembly should be expanded to 35 members and more support should be provided to community councils.

"The current community councils provide a valuable channel for community engagement on local planning and related issues. However, their effectiveness is often affected by a lack of government-funded secretariat services," the party's submission said.

The call for a major review was met with a lukewarm response from the ACT Labor government, which said the existing arrangements had delivered strong economic growth and high living standards.

"Any major governance change would require clear evidence, community support and broad political consensus," an ACT government spokeswoman said.

Mr Smith said a rates-equivalent payment, quarantined from GST calculations, would better replace an existing federal municipal services payment to the ACT that he argued had not kept up with costs.

The submission said the municipal payment was $21.6 million in 1988-89, about $61 million in today's dollars. In 2025-26, it was $46.3 million.

"Per Canberran, that is a fall from about $220 to $95 in today's dollars. Had the payment simply held its 1988-89 value per head, it would be worth about $108 million this year, more than double what is paid, and the cumulative shortfall against even its starting real value is more than $200 million," Mr Smith said.

"In real terms the Commonwealth's recognition of the territory's municipal disabilities has fallen by about a quarter since self-government, in a city whose population has grown by about three quarters."

Mr Smith has told the inquiry examining political representation in the ACT it should recommend a federal parliamentary inquiry into the system of self government and ask the federal government for an independently assessed payment to better cover the cost of municipal services in the capital.

Federal Labor MP David Smith. Picture by Keegan Carroll

"The Self-Government Act is an act of the Federal Parliament. The Commonwealth's exemption from territory taxes rests on Commonwealth law. The payment that offsets the ACT's municipal disabilities is a Commonwealth payment," Mr Smith said.

"An ACT federal member has a proper interest in whether those arrangements are working, and a proper role in asking the Federal Parliament to look at them."

Mr Smith's 32-page submission to the Legislative Assembly inquiry into electoral representation makes six recommendations and sets out the history of funding arrangements, arguing the ACT's inability to tax Commonwealth land or wages has short-changed the territory.

The Labor MP said the size of the Legislative Assembly should not be examined in isolation and any assessment of the number of political representatives the ACT needed ought to also account for the way the territory was funded.

"Self-government has served Canberra well. Support for self-government should not require support for every aspect of a settlement made nearly 40 years ago by people who, on their own account, were counting numbers rather than designing institutions, and only partly revisited since," he said.

Mr Smith said the impact on the ACT of the Commonwealth's exemption from paying rates or payroll tax was larger than other states faced because the Commonwealth was among the largest landowners and the largest employer.

"The exemption is not a fact of nature or a consequence of federation. It is a choice made in Commonwealth law, and it is a choice the Commonwealth could revisit," he said.
